I will keep all 6.0 mu in stevia this year. I have done this crop many years, so I do not start from zero. I start from what has worked in my fields and then adjust a little for cost, water, and yield. Since I have well irrigation, I can push the crop a bit more steadily than someone waiting on rain. My farm is not large, but 6 mu is enough that if I save too much on fertilizer and lose leaf yield, I will feel that loss much more than the extra few bags of input. So I will feed the crop on the safe side, but not blindly. Stevia needs the field to stay clean, loose, and supplied steadily, especially early growth and after cutting. I will use improved seedling material, because on a small-medium area like mine, uniform stand is worth the money. For tillage, I will use rotary tillage because it is enough for my land, it saves labor compared with deep ploughing every year, and it works well when I can irrigate after transplanting. On fertilizer, I will not chase very high nitrogen, because too much nitrogen can make the plants too soft and leafy without giving me the kind of leaf quality I want. But I also will not cut it too low. I will hold nitrogen at 12 kg per mu, phosphorus at 8 kg per mu, and potassium at 10 kg per mu. I will put most phosphorus and potassium in the base, then split nitrogen so the field does not run out after establishment. Water, I will plan for 5 irrigations across the season: one after transplanting, two in strong vegetative growth, one after the first big cut or regrowth period if needed, and one more if summer heat pulls moisture fast. For pests and disease, I will keep 3 sprays in mind for the year. If pressure stays light, I may not need every pass, but when I make the annual budget, I will reserve money for 3 applications because losing clean leaves is more expensive than one missed spray cost. With this plan, on my land and with decent management, I will target about 180 kg per mu.
